Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. A: ......  B: ......  C: ......  D: ......

What rule governs the formation of compound D from B? *[9 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Compound A is $\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}$ and its hydrolysis (step iii) gives $\mathrm{CH_3(CH_2)_3OH}$, butan-1-ol, so **A is 1-bromobutane**, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}$.

**(i)**

| | Reagent(s) | Reaction conditions |
|---|---|---|
| i | **ethanolic** potassium (or sodium) hydroxide, KOH in ethanol | heat under reflux (elimination of HBr) |
| ii | bromine, $\mathrm{Br_2}$ (liquid, or in tetrachloromethane; bromine water also decolourises) | room temperature, no catalyst (addition) |
| iii | **aqueous** sodium (or potassium) hydroxide, NaOH(aq) | heat under reflux (nucleophilic substitution) |
| iv | hydrogen chloride, HCl (gas or concentrated) | room temperature (addition) |

**(ii)**

- **A:** $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Br}$ (1-bromobutane)
- **B:** $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CH_2}$ (but-1-ene), $\mathrm{C_4H_8}$ formed by elimination of HBr
- **C:** $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHBrCH_2Br}$ (1,2-dibromobutane), $\mathrm{C_4H_8Br_2}$
- **D:** $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHClCH_3}$ (2-chlorobutane), $\mathrm{C_4H_9Cl}$, the major product

**Rule governing the formation of D from B: Markovnikov's rule.** When a hydrogen halide HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the **hydrogen atom goes to the carbon atom that already carries more hydrogen atoms** and the halogen to the carbon with fewer hydrogens, so that 2-chlorobutane (not 1-chlorobutane) is the major product. This is because the reaction goes through the more stable **secondary carbocation** ($\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH^+CH_3}$) rather than the primary one.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The compound $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}$ exhibits isomerism.

(i) What is isomerism?

(ii) Give all the position isomers of the compound.

(iii) Arrange the position isomers in order of increasing boiling point starting with the least.

Explain your trend.

(iv) State another kind of isomerism exhibited by the compound. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Isomerism is the existence of **two or more compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of the atoms** (different structural or spatial formulae), and therefore different properties.

**(ii)** The position isomers are the alcohols $\mathrm{C_4H_9OH}$ in which the $-\mathrm{OH}$ group is in different positions on the same carbon skeleton:

- on the straight chain: **butan-1-ol**, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH}$, and **butan-2-ol**, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3}$;
- on the branched skeleton: **2-methylpropan-1-ol**, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCH_2OH}$, and **2-methylpropan-2-ol**, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH}$.

**(iii)** Order of increasing boiling point (approximate values):

2-methylpropan-2-ol ($82\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) $<$ butan-2-ol ($99.5\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) $<$ 2-methylpropan-1-ol ($108\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) $<$ butan-1-ol ($118\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$)

**Explanation.** All four isomers form hydrogen bonds through the $-\mathrm{OH}$ group, but they differ in the strength of the **van der Waals forces** and in how easily the $-\mathrm{OH}$ group can take part in hydrogen bonding:

- A **straight chain** molecule (butan-1-ol) has the greatest surface area of contact between molecules, so the strongest van der Waals forces and the highest boiling point.
- **Branching** makes the molecule more compact (nearer to spherical), reducing the surface area of contact and the van der Waals forces, so the boiling point falls with increased branching.
- The $-\mathrm{OH}$ group of the **tertiary** alcohol is the most shielded by the three methyl groups, which hinders hydrogen bonding between molecules, so 2-methylpropan-2-ol boils lowest; the primary and secondary alcohols are less shielded.

**(iv)** **Functional group isomerism**: $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}$ also exists as **ethers**, e.g. ethoxyethane $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OCH_2CH_3}$ and methoxypropane $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_2CH_2CH_3}$. (Other kinds also shown by the compound: chain isomerism between butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol, and optical isomerism in butan-2-ol, which has an asymmetric carbon atom.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Give a chemical test that can be used to distinguish between butan-2-ol, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CH_3}$ and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $\mathrm{CH_3C(CH_3)(OH)CH_3}$. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Butan-2-ol is a **secondary** alcohol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is a **tertiary** alcohol; only the secondary alcohol is easily oxidised.

**Test: warm each alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution** ($\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7/H_2SO_4}$).

- **Butan-2-ol:** the orange solution turns **green** (the dichromate(VI) ion is reduced to $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$) as the alcohol is oxidised to the ketone butanone, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}$.
- **2-methylpropan-2-ol:** **no change**, the solution stays orange (a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised under these conditions).

(Alternatives: the iodoform test, warming with iodine and sodium hydroxide, gives a **yellow precipitate** of $\mathrm{CHI_3}$ with butan-2-ol, which contains the $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH){-}}$ group, but not with 2-methylpropan-2-ol; or the Lucas test, in which concentrated HCl with $\mathrm{ZnCl_2}$ turns the tertiary alcohol cloudy immediately and the secondary alcohol only after several minutes.)
